title: Psychosocial interventions and health-related quality of life in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
description:
Background. Type 1 diabetes (T1D) imposes substantial psychosocial demands on children, adolescents, and their families, and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is a key patient-centered outcome. Psychosocial interventions are recommended; however, their effects on HRQoL and their underlying principles remain unclear. We synthesized their effectiveness in HRQoL and characterized their theoretical foundations, components, targets, and delivery features.
Summary. Following PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420261349366), we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, EBSCO, and SCOPUS for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published between 2011 and March 2026 on psychosocial interventions in youth (≤18 years) with T1D reporting ≥1 HRQoL outcome. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, appraised interventions with the Theory Coding Scheme, and rated the quality with the NHLBI tool; a random-effects meta-analysis (Hedges' g) pooled trials with inactive comparators. Twelve reports (11 independent RCTs; 2,082 randomized participants) were included. Interventions drew on diverse traditions but shared components (psychoeducation, coping and problem-solving skills, communication and family engagement, and motivational and self-management strategies) and targets (self-efficacy, diabetes distress, family functioning, and self-management), with theory used descriptively rather than to test mechanisms. Across five trials (752 participants), interventions produced a small but statistically significant HRQoL improvement compared with inactive controls (Hedges' g = 0.24; 95% CI 0.10–0.38; p = .001; I² = 0%). Gains in emotional well-being, family functioning, and self-management outnumbered glucose improvements. 
Key Messages. Psychosocial interventions yield a small but reliable HRQoL improvement in children and adolescents living with T1D and rest on a narrow shared architecture. Future trials should specify HRQoL as a primary endpoint, adequately power it, and formally tes

title: Understanding acceptability of a brief intervention for intrusive thoughts: A mixed- methods study
description:
Intrusive thoughts (ITs) are common yet distressing experiences for many adolescents
and young adults. Brief, accessible interventions that provide psychoeducation and
coping strategies are needed, yet little is known about how youth perceive such
interventions. The present study examined both qualitative and quantitative indicators
of acceptability in adolescents and young adults with ITs who completed a digital
single-session intervention (SSI). The study aimed to gather intervention feedback and
determine whether symptom improvement and/or demographic factors predicted
acceptability. We conducted a secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial
comparing our SSI to an information-only control group in individuals aged 13-25,
focusing solely on acceptability factors of the SSI condition. Thematic analyses
revealed that young people with ITs prefer interventions that normalize the experience
of ITs, are emotionally validating, accessible and engaging, stimulate self-reflection,
and contain evidence-based strategies. Importantly, those who reported qualitatively
accepting the intervention were more likely to experience a reduction in hopelessness
symptoms at post-intervention; however, acceptability was not associated with distress
reduction. Of interest, those who identified as non-Caucasian were less likely to report
they had a positive intervention experience compared to Caucasian individuals.
Participants reported wanting more diverse examples of ITs to connect more with the
psychoeducation, as well as more personalized examples for validation. These findings
indicate acceptability factors and barriers that young adults with ITs experienced during
a brief SSI. Future studies, employing more diverse examples of ITs, will be crucial for
understanding further effects on acceptability and engagement.

title: Perceived Changes in Religious Cognitive Dissonance and Mental Health Among Former Members of High-Demand Religions: A Cross-Sectional Study
description:
Introduction: Recent advances in Cognitive Dissonance theory have clarified its broad applications and its mental health consequences when dissonance remains unresolved. However, this theory has rarely been tested quantitatively in the context of religious transitions, a major non-normative life event associated with negative mental health outcomes.
Methods: In a cross-sectional sample of 1,206 religious dones, or individuals who leave religion and do not plan to return, we extend cognitive dissonance theory by testing the conditions under which unresolved dissonance relates to perceived mental health. Participants retrospectively reported belief–behavior inconsistency and related discomfort before and after leaving, as well as current depression, anxiety, and perceived post-traumatic growth (PTG).
Results: Participants reported perceiving significant reductions in dissonance following deidentification. Greater reductions in inconsistency were associated with lower depression and anxiety, while perceived growth operated through reduced discomfort about that inconsistency. Religious demand moderated the association between discomfort and perceived growth.
Conclusion: These findings suggest that cognitive dissonance may both motivate major non-normative life events and shape their psychological consequences. For some individuals, leaving religion may improve mental health not simply because they leave, but because leaving allows them to reduce dissonance and live in greater alignment with their beliefs.

title: Sex Differences in Overhand Throwing are Completely Due to Socialization: A Blank Slate “Hypothesis” Unconstrained by Evidence
description: Contemporary evolutionary biology–including evolutionary psychology–assumes an interactionist framework, recognizing the importance of both biological (nature) and environmental (nurture) influences. Despite this scientific consensus, within women’s studies and gender studies, socialization-only explanations of sex differences in behavior persist. This commentary evaluates a recent prominent example: Anne Fausto-Sterling’s 2025 critique of our 2018 Quarterly Review of Biology thesis that the large human sex difference in overhand throwing partly reflects an evolved male adaptation. Fausto-Sterling (FS) argues that our ancestral selection scenarios are unrealistic and that, based on a qualitative study of ten infants, childhood throwing differences are fully explained by early socialization. We demonstrate that FS’s critique fails in several ways. First, FS’s objections about our evolutionary scenarios rely on flawed characterizations of the hunter-gatherer literature, ignoring our primary focus on ancestral combat and discounting cross-cultural data showing far greater male involvement in hunting. Second, FS erroneously implies that childhood throwing performance is our sole evidence, ignoring extensive data presented on elite athletic performance, cross-cultural consistency, prenatal hormone exposure, and distinct skeletal sexual dimorphisms. Finally, FS treats evolutionary and developmental processes as mutually exclusive, failing to recognize that evolutionary theory predicts that socialization will often mediate and amplify evolved behavioral predispositions. We conclude that the persistence of FS’s socialization-only, Blank Slate perspective can only be maintained by ignoring relevant evidence.

title: The latent geometry of dream content
description: Dreams provide a potential unique window into human cognition, yet it remains unclear whether dream content reflects structured representational organization or largely idiosyncratic expression. Here, we analyze a large-scale dataset of dream narratives (21,607 reports) using a transformer language model to construct a high-dimensional representational space of dreams, in which each report is mapped onto a vector. We ask whether this space is structured, and if so, how different sources of information are organized within it. We find that dream content exhibits a structured latent geometry: dreams produced by different individuals, as well as by individuals of different genders, occupy systematically distinct regions of this space, particularly in more abstract semantic representations. Temporal information is also embedded in this geometry: the similarity between dreams decreases gradually as the temporal distance between them increases, revealing a continuous encoding of historical proximity, although this effect mainly reflects changes in language use and narrative conventions over time. Finally, similarity among independent descriptions of dreamers predicts similarity in their dream content, linking person-level characteristics to the organization of dream representations. Together, these results show that dreams are not random constructions but structured expressions of latent cognitive organization, in which personal, demographic and historical dimensions are systematically embedded across multiple representational levels. By making this structure explicit, the present approach provides a general computational framework for mapping the organization of internal experience.

title: Measuring Intention: The Sense of Agency, Intentional Binding, and The Temporal Difference Limen
description: The sense of agency, the experience of controlling one’s actions and their outcomes, is essential to motor control, social cognition, and the design of assistive devices. Intentional binding (IB), the subjective compression in time between a voluntary action and its sensory outcome, is often used as a quantitative measure of agency. However, current IB methods are cognitively demanding, and recent studies suggest that temporal compression may reflect causal expectations rather than intention itself. To address this, we conducted a psychophysical two-alternative forced-choice study that isolated intention from causation by matching causal outcomes across conditions. Participants performed pairs of movements on a Kinarm device and judged which of two intervals between a visual cue at the end of movement and a post-movement tone was shorter. Pairs consisted of either active and passive movements (experimental group, n = 19) or two passive movements (control group, n = 19). We observed no group differences in time compression bias, defined as the point of subjective equality. In contrast, the experimental group showed significantly lower just-noticeable difference values than the control group (p < 0.01), reflecting a lower temporal difference limen (TDL). This finding suggests that the TDL may capture a link between intention and action and may serve as an implicit measure of the sense of agency. These results support recent claims that intentional binding may primarily reflect causal binding and provide evidence for TDL as a measure for evaluating the sense of agency.

title: Is There a Trade-Off Between Processing and Maintenance of Information in Working Memory?
description:
Working memory maintains information for ongoing processing. Concurrent maintenance and
processing often incur a cost: Processing can impair memory, and memory load can slow
processing responses. Such costs in complex-span tasks are often interpreted as shared-resource
competition. Alternatively, these costs may arise when processing requires additional information
to be encoded into working memory. Across three experiments, we tested these accounts with a
complex-span paradigm separating processing demand from encoding additional information.
Participants remembered novel objects while performing no processing, a constant response, a
size judgment on each object against a constant reference, or a size judgment against a changing
reference. Memory accuracy declined primarily when processing introduced a changing reference
object, not when processing demand increased alone. Memory load did not progressively impair
processing. These findings suggest that maintenance and processing are not generally constrained
by a shared resource; memory costs instead depend on whether processing introduces additional
representations.

title: Geographically aggregated psychological traits from linguistic analysis of Twitter data predict U.S. voter realignment since 2016
description:
The 2016 U.S. Presidential election heralded the beginning of a political realignment in American politics. A key question for understanding this realignment is whether the Republican party’s shift towards right-wing populism was driven by Donald Trump’s candidacy, versus Trump’s political success being driven by dynamics in the electorate that predated his political
rise. Individual surveys have commonly been used to address such questions, but there are many limitations to that method, including the cost of data collection and the need for accurate self-reflection on psychological questionnaires. We instead addressed this question by examining a corpus of Twitter posts written between July 2009 and February 2015, aggregated by U.S. county. The geographic distribution of psychological traits (personality, empathy, and moral foundations) was estimated by applying to the aggregated Twitter data lexica quantifying how strongly individual words predict psychological traits. The aggregate personality measures were then used to predict vote share for Donald Trump from 2016 to 2024, controlling for a baseline of prior Republican support. Low agreeableness predicts greater support for Trump, a novel result relative to other geographically aggregated data but consistent with prior survey findings relating this trait to right-wing populism. Low empathic concern and the degree to which tweets reference unfairness and defilement also predict shifts towards Trump. Our analysis suggests that people in geographic regions that shifted rightward beginning in 2016 were already expressing emotions consistent with Donald Trump’s messaging in their social media postings before his political rise.

title: Quality of Life in Middle and Later Life across Europe: Trait-Occasion Decomposition Using the Measurement-Aligned SHARE CASP-12
description: Quality of life (QoL) in middle and later life is widely assessed using the CASP scale, yet its measurement structure and comparability across groups and longitudinal waves remain contested. Using data from five waves of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), spanning nearly 10 years and 12 countries, this study examined the factor structure and measurement invariance of the SHARE CASP-12, applied a trait–state–occasion framework to distinguish stable trait-related from occasion-specific components of QoL, and assessed their social, economic, and health-related predictors. The results showed that the first-order three-factor model distinguishing Control/Autonomy, Pleasure, and Self-realization provided the best representation of the data. Scalar invariance was not supported across the grouping schemes examined, suggesting that unadjusted cross-group comparisons may be insufficiently justified. QoL comprised both stable and occasion-specific variation: Pleasure was predominantly occasion-specific, whereas Control/Autonomy and Self-realization were more trait-related. The relative contributions of these components varied across countries, sex, waves, and age. Education was more consistently associated with trait-related variation, while health status, chronic disease status, and household economic status showed more domain- and component-specific associations. Sensitivity analyses supported the main conclusions for Control/Autonomy and Self-realization, whereas findings for Pleasure were more sensitive to country composition. Overall, these results underscore the importance of measurement comparability and suggest that stable inequalities and shorter-term fluctuations in QoL may have distinct determinants.
